title: Born of tapas
hook: the power goes out on a night with no moon. In the creation hymn's dark, the One is born of tapas, heat: why Hindus fast and keep vows
carry: tapas: the holy heat of discipline
tomorrow: which comes first, a thought or a want?

segments.voice: Yesterday, That One: one reality, before every name. Before night or day, That One breathed without wind.

The power goes out on a night with no moon. You shut your eyes, then open them, and can't tell the difference. The dark behind your eyelids and the dark of the room have become one dark. Your hand is somewhere in front of your face, but you couldn't prove it. Nothing has an edge. The Nasadiya Sukta's third verse begins in that kind of dark, and pushes it further than any power cut could.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `EYES OPEN, EYES SHUT: THE SAME.` → `NOTHING HAS AN EDGE.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit the verse opens tama asit tamasa gulham agre. Darkness there was, hidden by darkness, in the beginning. Not darkness covering something: darkness covering darkness. Nothing to see, and nothing to see it with. In paraphrase it goes on: all this was water, with no mark on it, nothing told apart from anything else. That's the hymn's picture of the start: not an empty space with sharp edges, but a sameness so complete that nothing could stand out. Then the turn. What was coming into being lay covered by emptiness, and that One was born by the power of tapas. Tapas is a word for heat. And here's the part to tell a friend tonight: the same word names the heat a person builds through vows, fasting and long prayer. Notice what the verse leaves out. It doesn't say who made the heat, or name a god striking a spark. First, sameness, dark on dark. Then warmth. Then one thing that could be told apart. Later texts take the thread further. The Taittiriya Upanishad says the One wished to become many, performed tapas, and having done it, made all this. So when a grandmother fasts on Ekadashi, or a family keeps a vow through a festival, the tradition doesn't see mere going without. It sees tapas: the same warm power the world was born from, building in a person, and offered to God.
screen: `DARKNESS HIDDEN BY DARKNESS.` · `WATER WITH NO MARK ON IT.` · `THE ONE, BORN BY THE POWER OF TAPAS.` · `FASTS AND VOWS: TAPAS TODAY.` · then, large: `TAPAS: THE HOLY HEAT OF DISCIPLINE.`

segments.voice: Choose one small vow for today, the way families keep a vrata: one meal kept simple, no phone for the first hour, or one kind thing done without being thanked. Then close your eyes or lower your gaze, let the dark be plain, and find one warm place, the hands resting together or the middle of the chest. Rest there, holding the vow, coming back whenever a thought pulls you off. If you pray, offer the vow to God; if not, keep it for someone you love.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. In its third verse, darkness hidden by darkness, until the One was born by the power of heat.
Your line: tapas, the holy heat of discipline. First dark on dark, then warmth. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Many Hindus keep vratas, vows, and fasts such as Ekadashi, understood as tapas: a discipline offered to God. The Nasadiya Sukta itself is kept in traditional recitation, learned by memory from a teacher.

tapas.meaning: heat; later also the glow built by vows and discipline

tama asit tamasa gulham agre.meaning: darkness there was, hidden by darkness, in the beginning

Nasadiya Sukta.meaning: the Rig Veda's hymn of creation, named from its opening words

vrata.meaning: a religious vow, often a fast or a practice kept for a set time

Ekadashi.meaning: the eleventh day of each lunar fortnight, a common fast day, especially for Vishnu

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.129.3 (all this was undistinguished water; what was coming to be was covered by the void; that One was born by the power of tapas)
Taittiriya Upanishad 2.6 (he desired: may I be many; he performed tapas; having performed tapas, he created all this)

notes: Days 1250 (verse 1) and 1251 (verse 2) were checked after writing; this day takes verse 3, and 1253–1255 take verses 4, 5 and 6–7. The review picks up 1251.
Sanskrit of 10.129.3a (tama āsīt tamasā gūḷham agre) and 3d (tapasas tan mahinājāyataikam) given from memory in simplified transliteration; confirm.
Paraphrase of 3b–c: 'all this was water with no mark on it' (apraketaṃ salilam), 'what was coming into being lay covered by emptiness' (tucchyenābhv apihitam). Confirm.
Claim that later Hindu texts use tapas for the heat of vows, fasting and austerity: standard, but confirm the wording. No etymology is claimed.
The kitchen and blank-page images are offered as the writer's analogy, explicitly not as the hymn's meaning.
